titleEn: Shinu? Sudanese Arabic's short question
facts: Sudanese Arabic uses 'shinu' for 'what?', a compressed form that is one of the dialect's most recognisable words.
The dialect pronounces jim as g and qaf as g in many words, and it has absorbed vocabulary from Nubian, Beja and other Sudanese languages.
Sudanese speech is often described as slower and more sing-song than Egyptian Arabic, with distinctive greetings such as 'kefnak?' and 'kefik?'.
The dialect is the everyday language of Khartoum and much of the north, while southern Sudan has other languages and Juba Arabic as a lingua franca.
Sudanese songs and poetry frequently use dialect, and radio presenters switch between dialect and standard Arabic depending on the programme.
exampleEn: A Khartoum market seller calls out 'shinu ya bashmuhandis?' ('what do you need, engineer?') to a regular customer, using the dialect's habit of adding a joking title to the greeting.
qualificationEn: Sudanese Arabic covers a family of regional varieties, and the country's linguistic map includes Nubian, Beja, Fur and many other languages; 'shinu' is not equally common in every region.

titleEn: Barcha: Tunisian Arabic's word for plenty
facts: Barcha means 'a lot' or 'very much' in Tunisian Arabic, and it is used as an intensifier in everyday speech.
Tunisian Arabic is distinctive in the Maghreb for its heavy borrowing from French, Italian and Berber, and for its fast, clipped pronunciation.
Speakers often code-switch mid-sentence between Tunisian Arabic, French and standard Arabic, and the choice signals education, class or humour.
The dialect is not usually written in official contexts, so the same word may appear in many spellings when Tunisians text each other.
Tunisian television and music have spread some dialect words across the region, but barcha remains a marker of Tunisian identity.
exampleEn: A Tunisian friend asks how the wedding was and gets the answer 'barcha barcha' ('very, very much'); the repetition is the joke, and the speaker switches into French for the next sentence about the food.
qualificationEn: Tunisian Arabic is one dialect within a varied Maghrebi continuum, and barcha is not standard Arabic; Moroccans and Algerians may use different words for 'a lot'.

titleEn: Darija runs on two grammars at once
facts: Moroccan Arabic, called Darija, is the everyday spoken language of most Moroccans, while Modern Standard Arabic dominates official writing and formal speech.
Darija has absorbed a large French vocabulary from the protectorate period and a layer of Spanish in the north, plus Amazigh words from the languages spoken before Arabic arrived.
Code-switching is normal: a single sentence may contain Darija grammar, French nouns, Arabic connective phrases and an English brand name.
Moroccans write Darija in Arabic script, in Latin script with numbers for Arabic sounds, or not at all, and advertising often mixes scripts.
The dialect has no single standard, so spelling and vocabulary differ between Casablanca, Fez, Tangier and the south.
exampleEn: A Casablanca office worker tells a colleague 'wāsh bghīti n-dīr l-i rendez-vous?' ('do you want me to make an appointment?'), with the French word embedded in a Darija sentence and no pause for the switch.
qualificationEn: Darija is not a single uniform dialect, and many Moroccans switch between several registers during one day; literacy in standard Arabic still shapes formal and religious speech.

titleEn: Silaw: a Kurdish hello written in Arabic letters
facts: Sorani is a Kurdish dialect spoken mainly in Iraq and western Iran, and it is written in a modified Arabic script, unlike the Latin-script Kurmanji of Turkey and Syria.
The everyday greeting 'silaw' means 'hello' or 'be well', and it is used across Sorani-speaking areas alongside the Arabic 'salam'.
Sorani has its own literary tradition, with poetry, newspapers and school textbooks, and it is an official language of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.
Kurdish is an Indo-European language, so its grammar is not related to Arabic even though the two share vocabulary and script.
Many Iraqi Kurds are bilingual in Sorani and Arabic, and code-switching between them is common in offices and universities.
exampleEn: A student in Erbil greets a professor with 'silaw', then continues the conversation in Arabic when the professor asks about a form written in Arabic; the two languages share the sentence without friction.
qualificationEn: Kurdish is not a single language, and Sorani speakers may not easily understand Kurmanji; Arabic-script Sorani is also different from the Kurdish spoken in Turkey and Syria.

titleEn: Mahr: the marriage payment that is not a price
facts: Mahr is the payment a groom owes the bride under an Islamic marriage contract, and it can be paid in cash, gold, property or any agreed value.
It is usually split into an advance portion paid at the wedding and a deferred portion payable if the marriage ends or the husband dies.
The mahr belongs to the bride personally, not to her father, and it is recorded in the written contract.
It is often described as a bride price in English, but it is a right of the bride rather than a purchase of her, and it can be modest or symbolic.
Negotiations over mahr are a normal part of Egyptian and wider Arab marriage talks, and inflated demands have become a public complaint.
exampleEn: At a Cairo engagement, the two families agree on a mahr of a gold set plus a deferred sum recorded in the contract; the bride's mother notes the figure in a notebook, and the imam will read it aloud at the signing.
qualificationEn: Mahr practice varies widely by country, class and family, and it is not the same as the wedding expenses or the dowry brought by the bride; some couples agree on a token amount.

titleEn: The kunya: a parent renamed after a child
facts: A kunya is a teknonymy: a person is addressed as Abu (father of) or Umm (mother of) followed by the name of the eldest child, usually the son.
It is a mark of respect and familiarity, and using it instead of a first name can be warmer or more formal depending on the relationship.
Parents acquire the kunya after the birth of their first child, and it may change if the child's name is changed or if a later child becomes better known.
The device is also used as a pseudonym in politics and war, and many public figures are known mainly by their kunya.
A childless adult may still be given a kunya as a courtesy, and women often use one publicly even when their own name is well known.
exampleEn: A Riyadh office worker who has always been called Saad is addressed as 'Abu Faisal' after his son is born; colleagues switch within days, and only his mother still uses his first name.
qualificationEn: Kunya use varies by region and generation, and younger urban Saudis may use first names more often; the choice of the eldest child's name is a convention rather than a rule.

titleEn: The Eid visit: who goes to whom, and in what order
facts: Eid al-Fitr follows Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha follows the pilgrimage season; both begin with a morning prayer and a round of family visits.
The usual order is grandparents first, then parents and siblings, then aunts, uncles and close friends, with the eldest relatives receiving visits rather than making them.
Children receive Eidi, cash gifts that can be a significant sum for a child and a source of competition among cousins.
In Egypt many families visit cemeteries before or after Eid to clean graves and recite Quran, a custom that mixes celebration with mourning.
The visit is short and formulaic: greetings, sweets, tea, a report on the family's news, and a promise to meet again; staying too long is a minor social error.
exampleEn: On the first morning of Eid in Cairo, a family drives to the grandmother's flat at nine, eats kahk and drinks tea, then makes two shorter visits to uncles before lunch; the children count their Eidi in the car.
qualificationEn: Eid visiting customs differ between the two Eids and between countries, and many families now spread visits over several days or replace them with phone calls; the cemetery visit is common in Egypt but not universal.

titleEn: The cup that is never filled: qahwa service
facts: Arabic coffee, qahwa, is brewed from lightly roasted beans with cardamom and sometimes saffron or cloves, and it is served in small handleless cups called finjan.
It is poured from a long-spouted dallah, always with the right hand, and the cup is filled only a third full so that the guest can drink it hot and accept a refill.
The serving order follows seniority and status, and it is the youngest or a servant who carries the dallah, not the host.
A guest signals that they have had enough by shaking the cup gently from side to side; handing the cup back full is a silent refusal.
Qahwa is served at weddings, funerals, business meetings and ordinary visits, and the ritual is as important as the drink.
exampleEn: At a funeral in Riyadh, a boy walks the row of seated men with a dallah and a stack of cups; each man takes one with his right hand, drinks, and shakes the cup when he is finished, and the boy moves on without a word.
qualificationEn: Coffee ritual varies across the Gulf and the Levant: cardamom-heavy qahwa is typical of the Gulf, while Levantine coffee is usually served in larger cups and without cardamom; Turkish-style coffee is common in cities.

titleEn: Mansaf: one platter, many hands
facts: Mansaf is Jordan's national dish: lamb cooked in jameed, a hard dried yoghurt, and served over rice and thin shrak bread.
It is traditionally eaten from a single large platter, with guests using their right hand to roll rice and meat into a ball.
The dish is the standard hospitality meal for weddings, funerals, tribal gatherings and religious holidays, and serving it signals that the host is honouring the guests.
The jameed is made by salting and drying goat's or sheep's milk, then soaking and blending it into the cooking liquid.
A whole lamb on top of the rice is the most prestigious presentation, and the best pieces are offered to the most senior guest.
exampleEn: At a Jordanian wedding in Karak, the host's family sets down a platter for eight men; an uncle tears the meat and rolls rice, the eldest guest is offered the first bite, and the meal ends with tea and thanks to the host's ancestors.
qualificationEn: Mansaf is strongly associated with Jordan but is also eaten in parts of Syria and Palestine; the dish's prestige and the size of the gathering depend on the family and the occasion, and younger urban families sometimes serve it plated.

titleEn: Mezze is a conversation, not a starter
facts: Mezze is a spread of many small dishes served at the start of a Levantine meal or as the meal itself, with hummus, mutabbal, tabbouleh, kibbeh, pickles and olives as staples.
In Lebanon and Syria it is often eaten with arak, an aniseed spirit diluted with water, and the meal can last for hours.
The dishes are placed in the centre of the table and shared, and the host keeps adding plates until the guests refuse.
Mezze is a restaurant institution as well as a home practice, and Beirut's restaurants compete on the number and quality of cold and hot dishes.
The word is used across the region, but its content and order differ: in Greece and Turkey, meze is a smaller accompaniment to drinks rather than the main event.
exampleEn: A Sunday lunch in a Lebanese village begins with twelve cold dishes and a bottle of arak; the men talk and eat slowly, the host's mother sends out hot kibbeh in rounds, and nobody mentions the main course until two hours have passed.
qualificationEn: Mezze is not uniform across the Levant, and its role changes between home and restaurant; a home meal may have only three or four dishes, while a restaurant mezze can run to twenty.

titleEn: Pouring mint tea from a height
facts: Maghrebi mint tea is green tea with fresh spearmint and a large amount of sugar, and it is the standard drink of hospitality in Morocco.
It is poured from a height so that the stream aerates the tea and creates a thin foam, and the pour is a performance that guests watch.
The usual gesture is three glasses: the first is said to be bitter like life, the second sweet like love, and the third gentle like death.
The tea is served in small decorated glasses, and refusing it or commenting on its sweetness is a social statement.
Families buy mint by the bunch at the market, and the quality of the tea and the quantity of sugar are measures of how the host values the guest.
exampleEn: On a rooftop in Fez, the host lifts the teapot a metre above the glass, pours a long stream, and hands the first glass to the oldest guest; the foam settles, and the conversation resumes only after everyone has drunk.
qualificationEn: The three-glass explanation is a popular saying rather than a rule, and the strength and sweetness of the tea vary by region and family; in Algeria and Tunisia the same ritual exists with local variations.

titleEn: Couscous belongs to Friday
facts: Couscous is steamed semolina served with meat, vegetables and a broth, and in the Maghreb it is traditionally the Friday lunch after the mosque.
The grain is rolled by hand from semolina and water, then steamed three times, which makes it light and separate rather than sticky.
Families eat from a shared platter, and the cook's skill is judged by the fineness of the grain and the balance of the broth.
Each country has its own versions: Moroccan couscous is often sweeter and uses seven vegetables, Algerian and Tunisian versions differ in spicing and in the meat used.
The dish is also a diaspora staple, and Friday couscous in Paris or Marseille is a way of keeping the family calendar.
exampleEn: In a Casablanca house, the grandmother steams the couscous over the broth while the men return from Friday prayer; the platter is placed in the middle of the table, and everyone eats from the same mound with a spoon or by hand.
qualificationEn: Couscous is eaten on other days too, and the Friday tradition is strongest in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia; the recipe and the vegetables change with the season and the family's budget.

titleEn: The fanous: a lantern children carry through Ramadan
facts: Fanous Ramadan is a lantern associated with the month of Ramadan, and it is especially linked to Egypt, where the tradition is said to go back to the Fatimid period.
Children carry the lanterns through the streets after iftar, sing Ramadan songs and compare designs; the classic form is coloured glass and metal.
The most famous song, 'Wahawi ya wahawi', is sung by children during the month and has dozens of verses.
Modern fanous are often battery-powered plastic, but craftsmen in Cairo still make the traditional glass and tin versions for wealthier buyers.
Lanterns also decorate balconies, shop windows and mosque courtyards, and the first night of Ramadan is marked by their appearance.
exampleEn: On the first night of Ramadan in a Cairo neighbourhood, a grandmother gives her grandson a red-and-green glass fanous; he walks the alley with friends, singing the 'wahawi' song, and the adults sit on the doorstep watching.
qualificationEn: The fanous is an Egyptian tradition that has spread across the Arab world, but its form and importance vary; in some countries lanterns are decorative only, and many families now use LED versions.

titleEn: Gargee'an: the door-to-door nights of Ramadan
facts: Gargee'an is a Gulf celebration in which children dress in traditional clothes and go door to door on the 13th, 14th and 15th nights of Ramadan.
Neighbours fill their bags with sweets, nuts and coins, and the children sing a short song that names the house and asks for treats.
The custom is strongest in Kuwait, Bahrain, eastern Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and it has a Sha'ban counterpart in some communities.
Households prepare baskets of sweets in advance, and the size of the bag a child brings home is a small marker of neighbourhood generosity.
In Iraq, a related tradition is called Girgian or Qarqe'an, with similar door-to-door visits and songs.
exampleEn: In a Kuwaiti neighbourhood on the 14th night of Ramadan, a group of children in embroidered clothes knock on doors, sing 'gargee'an, gargee'an', and come home with bags of nuts and sweets that their mothers sort on the kitchen table.
qualificationEn: Gargee'an is a Gulf tradition with local names and dates, and not every family participates; in mixed expatriate neighbourhoods the door-to-door practice may be limited to Gulf households.

titleEn: Mawlid: the saint's birthday and the street fair
facts: Mawlid is the celebration of the Prophet Muhammad's birthday on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, observed across the Muslim world with public holidays, processions and sweets.
Egypt adds a second layer of mawlids for local saints, when entire neighbourhoods gather at a shrine with music, food stalls and rides.
The Cairo mawlid season includes famous celebrations such as Sayyida Zeinab and al-Hussein, where Sufi orders chant and families camp for days.
Halawet al-mawlid, a sweet made of semolina, nuts and syrup, and a decorated doll made of sugar or felt are sold in the streets for children.
Some Sunni reformist movements reject mawlid celebrations as an innovation, while Sufi orders treat them as central acts of devotion.
exampleEn: During the mawlid of Sayyida Zeinab in Cairo, a family buys halawet al-mawlid and a sugar doll for the children, walks through the crowded square and stops to listen to a Sufi chanting group outside the mosque.
qualificationEn: Mawlid practices differ widely between countries and between Sunni and Shia communities, and not all Muslims celebrate it; the Egyptian saint mawlids are a local tradition that is distinct from the Prophet's birthday.

titleEn: Ashura: the street becomes a mourning procession
facts: Ashura falls on the 10th of Muharram and commemorates the death of Hussein, the Prophet's grandson, at Karbala in 680.
In Iraq, Shia communities mark it with processions, black banners, latmiya poetry and ritual mourning, and some men perform tatbir, self-flagellation with blades.
Karbala and Najaf receive millions of pilgrims, and many Iraqis walk for days to reach the shrines.
Arba'een, forty days after Ashura, is one of the largest annual pilgrimages in the world, with processions and free food stations along the route.
Sunni Muslims generally mark Ashura with fasting, and the difference in practice is one of the visible distinctions between the two communities.
exampleEn: In a Baghdad street during Muharram, a procession of men in black beats their chests in rhythm while a loudspeaker carries a latmiya poem; a stall beside them hands out water and dates to anyone walking past, regardless of sect.
qualificationEn: Ashura practice varies sharply between Shia communities in Iraq, Iran, Lebanon and the Gulf, and between Sunni and Shia observance; media images of self-flagellation are only one part of a much broader ritual calendar.
